meta.name: Cardiac Arrest with Unverified DNR — Verbal Claim Only, When in Doubt Resuscitate

patient.name: Henry Aldrich
patient.chiefComplaint: Found unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless in his hospital bed at home. Family states he has a DNR but cannot produce any document or bracelet.

history.hpi: 88-year-old male with end-stage congestive heart failure, found unresponsive in his home hospital bed this morning when his son came in with his morning pills at approximately 07:45. He was last seen awake and in his usual state of health at about 22:00 last night when his wife helped him settle for bed — downtime is therefore unknown and the arrest is unwitnessed. The son reports his father's health has been declining for months; he sleeps in a hospital bed in the back bedroom and needs help with most daily activities. The son states firmly that his father has a signed DNR — "His doctor signed it. He wanted to pass peacefully" — but when asked for the paperwork he says it must be with the lawyer or in a safe deposit box. No physical DNR, POLST, or advance directive document can be produced on scene, the patient wears no identification bracelet on either wrist, and no one on scene presents healthcare power of attorney documentation. No bystander CPR has been performed.
pastMedical: End-stage congestive heart failure (per family, ejection fraction "very low")
Coronary artery disease — myocardial infarction approximately 10 years ago
COPD, on home oxygen at night
Osteoarthritis; largely bed-bound for the past two months
history.lastOralIntake: Small dinner around 18:00 last night; nothing since. He was found before taking his morning pills.
history.events: Wife helped him to bed around 22:00 last night — his usual baseline. Son entered the bedroom at approximately 07:45 with his morning pills and could not wake him, saw no breathing, and called 911. No bystander CPR initiated. Family met the crew at the door stating he has a DNR and "would not want you to do anything."

scene.dispatch: Medic 8, respond to 333 Serenity Lane for an 88-year-old male, unresponsive. The caller states they cannot wake the patient. Time out is 07:51.
scene.location: Well-kept single-family home. The patient is in a back bedroom, lying supine in a hospital bed. Home oxygen concentrator in the corner (nasal cannula draped on the headboard, not on the patient), pill organizer and water glass on the nightstand. The room is quiet and calm.
scene.time: Weekday morning; dispatched 07:51, on scene approximately 07:58
scene.safety: No physical hazards. The scene is emotionally charged rather than dangerous: the family is calm, somber, and firmly opposed to resuscitation. The challenge is managing the family's wishes and the crew's legal duty at the same time — expect resistance to be verbal and grief-driven, not violent.
scene.bystanders: The patient's son, a man in his 50s, meets the crew at the front door — calm but somber: "Thank you for coming so quickly. That's my father, Henry. We tried to wake him for his morning pills, and he's completely unresponsive. I don't think he's breathing. Before you go in, you need to know he has a DNR. He would not want you to do anything." When asked for the paperwork or a bracelet: "Well, I don't have it in my hand. It must be with his lawyer or in their safe deposit box. But I am telling you, he has one. His doctor signed it. He wanted to pass peacefully." The patient's wife, also elderly, sits in a chair at the bedside holding her husband's hand and says softly: "Please... no heroics. It's not what he wanted."
visualCues: Elderly male lying supine in a hospital bed, completely still — no chest rise
Skin pale with cyanosis around the lips
No identification bracelet on either wrist; nothing posted on the wall, refrigerator, or nightstand
No DNR, POLST, or advance directive paperwork anywhere in view
No rigor, no dependent lividity — obvious-death criteria are NOT met
Home oxygen concentrator, hospital bed, pill organizer — a chronically ill patient cared for at home
Wife seated at the bedside holding the patient's hand; son standing in the doorway
Warm indoor environment — no reason to suspect hypothermia

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: An 88-year-old man is pulseless and apneic in a hospital bed, and standing between the crew and the patient is a calm, sincere, grieving son saying the words that make this a summative: "he has a DNR." Nobody on this scene is lying — the family is probably right that a document exists somewhere — but MATC's DNR/advance-directives protocol is unambiguous about what counts: the document (or a state-sanctioned identification bracelet) must be IMMEDIATELY AVAILABLE, and it is only valid if it conforms to state specifications, is intact, and displays the patient's name. A verbal report of a DNR in a safe deposit box meets none of that. The protocol also names the crew's move when validity is in question: proceed with the resuscitation until additional information clarifies the best course of action — and its Patient Safety Consideration says it even more plainly: when the appropriateness of withholding resuscitation is questioned, initiate CPR immediately and contact medical direction. Meanwhile the cardiac arrest protocol demands the assessment stay focused — just enough to reveal pulselessness — with all further history gathered from the family WHILE treatment is ongoing. One more protocol nuance the source material glosses over: MATC recognizes that, in the absence of written directions, a person holding healthcare power of attorney may prescribe limits of treatment as specified from state to state — so the crew should ask; here, no one on scene has POA documentation either. The crew that passes this scenario confirms the arrest in seconds, asks one clear question about paperwork, explains their obligation with empathy, and puts hands on the chest.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Open when positioned; no secretions, no obstruction visible; no spontaneous respirations
clinicalPresentation.breathing: APNEIC — no chest rise or fall observed; no breath sounds on auscultation
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No carotid pulse palpable on a deliberate 10-second check; skin pale, cyanosis around the lips
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Flaccid; no spontaneous movement; no response to painful stimulus
otherFindings: Unwitnessed arrest — last seen at baseline ~22:00 last night; downtime unknown
No bystander CPR prior to arrival
No DNR/POLST document, no identification bracelet on either wrist, no POA paperwork on scene
No rigor, no lividity — this is a workable arrest, not an obvious death
Son at the doorway: "I am telling you, he has one. His doctor signed it."
Wife at the bedside, softly: "Please... no heroics. It's not what he wanted."
Warm indoor environment — no evidence or suspicion of hypothermia

expectedActions.shortAction: Focused assessment — confirm apnea and pulselessness in seconds, not minutes
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Assessment 1–3 — the assessment is deliberately limited to revealing pulselessness, and everything else (including the DNR conversation) happens while treatment is ongoing. A crew that stands at the door negotiating before anyone has touched the patient has inverted the protocol's order of operations.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assessment: The patient in cardiac arrest requires a prompt balance of treatment and assessment. In cases of cardiac arrest, assessments should be focused and limited to obtaining enough information to reveal the patient is pulseless. Once pulselessness is discovered, treatment should be initiated immediately, and any further history must be obtained by bystanders while treatment is ongoing.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ask for the physical DNR document or identification bracelet — it must be immediately available
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Inclusion Criteria 1 — the protocol's entry requirement is a document or valid alternative (such as an identification bracelet) IMMEDIATELY AVAILABLE. Asking one clear, respectful question — "Do you have the paperwork here, or is he wearing a bracelet?" — is both the empathetic move and the protocol-required verification step. A claim about a lawyer's office or a safe deposit box does not satisfy it.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria: Patients must have one of the following documents or a valid alternative (such as identification bracelet indicating wishes) immediately available. Note that some specifics can vary widely from state to state: Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order – identifies that CPR and intubation are not to be initiated if the patient is in arrest or peri-arrest. The interventions covered by this order and the details around when to implement them can vary widely.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ask whether anyone present holds healthcare power of attorney documentation
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Inclusion Criteria 1d — in the absence of written directions, a person with healthcare power of attorney or healthcare proxy may prescribe limits of treatment as specified from state to state. The son is not claiming POA and has no such documentation, so this avenue closes too — but the crew should ask, because it is the one protocol-recognized way a person (rather than a paper) can limit treatment.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: As specified from state to state, in the absence of formal written directions (MOLST, POLST, DNR, advanced directives), and in the presence of a person with power of attorney for healthcare or healthcare proxy, that person may prescribe limits of treatment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Know what a VALID order requires: state specifications, intact, patient's name displayed
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Inclusion Criteria 2 — even a produced document must meet all three validity criteria before it becomes a "valid exclusion to resuscitation." This is why the crew can explain, without arguing, exactly what they would need to see: an intact, state-conforming order with the patient's name on it.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: One of the documents above is valid when it meets all the following criteria: Conforms to the state specifications for color and construction; Is intact: it has not been cut, broken or shows signs of being repaired; Displays the patient's name and, if required by state law or regulation, the physician's name.

expectedActions.shortAction: No document produced — proceed with resuscitation until the question is clarified
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Inclusion Criteria 3 and Patient Safety Considerations — the protocol answers this scenario's central question in one sentence: when validity is in question, resuscitate, and sort out the rest with medical direction. The crew explains this to the family with empathy ("I understand this is difficult; without the signed order here, we are required to begin") and moves to the chest. Delay is the failure mode.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If there is question about the validity of the form/instrument, the best course of action is to proceed with the resuscitation until additional information can be obtained to clarify the best course of action. Patient Safety Considerations: In cases where the patient's status is unclear and the appropriateness of withholding resuscitation efforts is questioned, EMS personnel should initiate CPR immediately and contact medical direction.

transitions.condition: The crew confirms apnea and pulselessness, respectfully asks for the physical DNR document or bracelet, and — when nothing can be produced — explains their obligation to the family and immediately begins high-quality chest compressions while the second crew member sets up the AED.

The crew accepts the family's verbal statement that a DNR exists and withholds CPR without any physical order, bracelet, or POA documentation being produced. They stand by the bedside, unsure, while no resuscitation occurs and downtime accumulates.

phases.name: Resuscitation initiated
phases.description: The crew has made the correct call: with no valid exclusion to resuscitation immediately available, this is a cardiac arrest like any other, and the cardiac arrest protocol takes over. One provider delivers continuous, high-quality compressions — 100 to 120 per minute, 2 to 2.4 inches, full recoil — while the other applies the AED pads and analyzes. The AED announces: "No shock advised." That changes the emphasis, not the effort — asystole earns no shock and an immediate return to the chest, with analysis repeating every two minutes and compressions continuing right up to each analysis. The airway is managed in a way that never interrupts the chest: passive oxygenation by NRB over an OPA, or BVM ventilation timed to the compression rhythm. In-line capnography on the ventilation circuit gives the crew the protocol's objective measure of compression quality. The family is still in the room — the son repeating that the DNR is real, the wife quietly holding her husband's hand — and the crew keeps working while keeping them informed. History continues to be gathered from the family exactly as the protocol directs: while treatment is ongoing.
phases.triggerCondition: No valid DNR document, bracelet, or POA documentation could be produced. The crew explained their obligation to the family, began high-quality chest compressions, and applied the AED — rhythm analysis returns "No shock advised."

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA in place, no gag reflex; airway patent with adjunct
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic — ventilations provided by crew without interrupting compressions
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No spontaneous pulse; compressions produce a palpable femoral pulsation; EtCO2 24 mmHg with good compressions
otherFindings: AED analysis: "No shock advised" — compressions resumed immediately
EtCO2 24 mmHg — compressions are effective (protocol floor is 10 mmHg)
Son, from the doorway: "He didn't want this. I told you he has a DNR." — crew acknowledges and continues
Additional history gathered from family WHILE treatment is ongoing, per protocol
No evidence or suspicion of hypothermia — house is warm
Engine 4 has been dispatched and is minutes out

expectedActions.shortAction: Begin chest compressions immediately while the second rescuer sets up the AED
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 1 and 1d — no bystander CPR has been performed and the arrest is unwitnessed, so compressions start immediately and continue while the AED is retrieved and applied. Compressions and defibrillation readiness happen in parallel, not in sequence.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Initiate chest compressions in cases with no bystander chest compressions or take over compressions from bystanders while a second rescuer is setting up the AED or defibrillator. For adults and children with unwitnessed cardiac arrest or for whom an AED is not immediately available, it is reasonable that CPR be initiated while the defibrillator equipment is being retrieved and applied and that defibrillation, if indicated, be attempted as soon as the device is ready for use.

expectedActions.shortAction: Compressions 100–120/min, 2–2.4 inches deep, full recoil, minimal interruptions
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Considerations 1 — the protocol defines effective compressions numerically, and everything else in the resuscitation is built around not interrupting them. In asystole there is no shock to deliver; compression quality IS the therapy.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Effective chest compressions are defined as: A rate of greater than 100 and less than 120 compressions/minute; Depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) and less than 2.4 inches (6 cm) for adults and children; Allow for complete chest recoil (avoid leaning); Minimize interruptions in compressions; Avoid rescuer fatigue by rotating rescuers at least every 2 minutes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply AED pads and analyze — no shock advised; resume 2-minute compression cycles
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 6 and Key Considerations 7 — the cycle is two minutes of compressions, then rhythm analysis, defibrillating only shockable rhythms. "No shock advised" means an immediate return to the chest; compressions continue between analysis and any charging.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Continue the cycle of chest compressions for 2 minutes, followed by rhythm analysis and defibrillation of shockable rhythms. Continue chest compressions between completion of AED analysis and AED charging.

expectedActions.shortAction: Manage airway without interrupting compressions — passive O2 via NRB/OPA or BVM per protocol options
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 6a–6b — in adult arrest the airway is deliberately secondary to compressions and defibrillation. The protocol offers passive ventilation (NRB over an OPA for the first 3–4 cycles), BVM at 10 breaths/minute on the upstroke, or 30:2 — any of them is acceptable; interrupting the chest for any of them is not.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The airway management strategy should not interrupt compressions. Passive ventilation: High flow oxygen is applied via a non-rebreather mask with an oropharyngeal airway. This may be applied for the first 3–4 compression cycles (6–8 minutes). BVM ventilation at 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 10 compressions), applied during the upstroke between compressions, without interrupting the compressions. BVM ventilation with 30:2 ventilation to compression ratio.

expectedActions.shortAction: Place an OPA (no gag reflex); provide maximal oxygen supplementation during CPR
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 2b and 3c — the OPA is the correct adjunct for a patient without a gag reflex, and during CPR the protocol calls for maximal oxygen supplementation rather than titration.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: During CPR, maximal oxygen supplementation should be provided. Oropharyngeal airways (OPA) or nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) can be placed if needed to maintain a patent airway and make BVM ventilation more effective: OPA are used for patients without gag reflex; NPA are used for patients with gag reflex.

expectedActions.shortAction: Capnography in line on the BVM — improve compression quality if EtCO2 falls below 10 mmHg
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Considerations 3 — quantitative EtCO2 is the objective feedback loop on compression quality; the protocol ties it to CPR effectiveness, not to advanced airway placement. It will matter again later: it is an early ROSC indicator and feeds the termination discussion if efforts remain ineffective.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Quantitative end-tidal capnography (EtCO2) should be used to monitor effectiveness of chest compressions: If EtCO2 less than 10 mmHg during the initial phases of resuscitation, attempt to improve chest compression quality.

transitions.condition: Immediately after compressions are underway and AED pads are placed, Engine 4 arrives on scene with a four-person crew. The lead student must assign pit-crew roles — compressors, ventilations, family support, and code leader — to convert the extra hands into an organized resuscitation.

phases.name: Engine crew delegated
phases.description: "Engine 4 is here." Four more sets of hands just walked into a small bedroom, and what happens next determines whether this becomes a high-performance resuscitation or a crowd. MATC's answer is the pit-crew model: two rescuers on opposite sides of the chest alternating compressions every 100 to avoid fatigue, dedicated hands on two-person BVM ventilation, a crew member supporting the family, and one clinician — the code leader — stepping back to oversee the entire response rather than performing tasks. The protocol also tells the crew what NOT to do yet: avoid advanced airway placement during the first four cycles (~10 minutes) — the OPA/BVM strategy continues — and do not package or move the patient, because compressions during movement lose depth, rate, and recoil; the resuscitation happens right here in the bedroom. The AED advises no shock at every 2-minute analysis. With the resuscitation now running itself, the DNR question is still open — and the code leader's next move is the one the protocol names explicitly: contact medical direction. Delegation is what buys the code leader the freedom to make that call.
phases.triggerCondition: Engine 4 arrives immediately after compressions are underway and pads are placed. The lead student assigns pit-crew roles: two engine firefighters alternate compressions, one manages two-person BVM ventilations with the partner, one supports the family, and the lead student assumes code leader.

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA in place; BVM ventilation coordinated with compressions, no interruptions
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic — ventilated by crew; equal chest rise with BVM
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No spontaneous pulse; continuous compressions with rescuers alternating every 100 compressions; EtCO2 26 mmHg
otherFindings: AED analysis at each 2-minute cycle: "No shock advised" every time
EtCO2 26 mmHg with rotated, fresh compressors
Two-person BVM ventilation with engine crew — equal chest rise, no interruption to compressions
Roles assigned and verbalized — no duplicated or missed tasks
Patient remains where found — no packaging or movement during resuscitation
Son has stepped into the hallway with a firefighter, on the phone trying to reach the father's lawyer about the DNR
Wife remains seated, holding the patient's hand; a crew member keeps her informed

expectedActions.shortAction: Assign pit-crew roles: alternating compressors, ventilations, family support, code leader oversight
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Considerations 14 — the pit-crew model with predefined roles is the protocol's answer to a multi-agency scene. The lead student's job shifts from doing tasks to running the code; failure to delegate produces exactly the disorganized, duplicated-effort resuscitation this summative is designed to expose.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ideally, clinicians in each EMS agency will use a "pit crew" approach when using this protocol to ensure the most effective and efficient cardiac arrest care. Rescuer 1 and 2 set up on opposite sides of patient's chest and perform continuous chest compressions, alternating after every 100 compressions to avoid fatigue. One responding clinician assumes code leader position overseeing the entire response. Use a CPR checklist to ensure that all best practices are followed during CPR.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rotate compressors at least every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue and quality decay
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Considerations 1e — compression quality degrades before the compressor feels it. With six providers on scene there is no excuse for a fatigued rescuer on the chest.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Avoid rescuer fatigue by rotating rescuers at least every 2 minutes. Some EMS pit crew approaches use a clinician on either side of the chest, alternating compressions every minute or every 100 compressions to avoid fatigue.

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue 2-minute cycles; pause only for AED analysis — no shock advised persists
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 6 and Key Considerations 14a-iii — the machine of the code: two minutes on the chest, analyze, back on the chest. Compressions are interrupted for rhythm checks and shocks only, and "no shock advised" earns an immediate return to compressions.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Continue the cycle of chest compressions for 2 minutes, followed by rhythm analysis and defibrillation of shockable rhythms. Chest compressions are only interrupted during rhythm check (AED analysis or manual) and defibrillation shocks – Continue compressions when AED/defibrillator is charging.

expectedActions.shortAction: Two-person BVM with engine support — just enough volume for visible chest rise
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Airway Management Treatment 4 — with the engine crew on scene there are enough hands for the preferred two-person, two-thumbs-up technique, and the volume target keeps the crew from overventilating a patient in arrest.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation in the setting of respiratory failure or arrest. Two-person, two-thumbs-up BVM ventilation is preferred. Ventilate with just enough volume to see chest rise, approximately 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight.

expectedActions.shortAction: Stay with OPA/BVM — avoid advanced airway placement during first four cycles (~10 min)
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Considerations 14a-v — the pit-crew model defers any advanced airway (including a supraglottic airway) through the first four cycles. For this crew that means the OPA/BVM strategy already working continues for the remainder of the scenario window; nothing about the airway interrupts the chest.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: During the first four cycles of compressions/defibrillation (approximately 10 minutes) avoid advanced airway placement.

expectedActions.shortAction: Resuscitate on scene — do not package or move the patient during the code
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Patient Safety Considerations — compressions during movement lose hands-on time, depth, recoil, and rate, and a moving code endangers the crew. The bedroom is the resuscitation room.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Performing manual chest compressions in a moving vehicle may pose a clinician safety concern. In addition, manual chest compressions during patient movement are less effective in regard to hands on time, depth, recoil and rate. Ideally, patients should be resuscitated as close to the scene as operationally possible.

expectedActions.shortAction: Code leader steps aside and contacts medical direction about the unverified DNR
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Patient Safety Considerations — the protocol pairs its two imperatives in a single sentence: initiate CPR immediately AND contact medical direction. Delegation has freed the code leader to give a clear, concise report: unwitnessed arrest, no shock advised at every AED analysis, high-quality CPR and BVM ventilation in progress, family alleging a DNR that cannot be produced. Medical control is the protocol-named resource for exactly this medico-legal gray zone.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: In cases where the patient's status is unclear and the appropriateness of withholding resuscitation efforts is questioned, EMS personnel should initiate CPR immediately and contact medical direction.

transitions.condition: With the engine crew running compressions and ventilations under pit-crew roles, the lead student steps aside and contacts medical control with a concise report of the arrest, the resuscitation in progress, and the family's unverified DNR claim.

phases.name: Medical control contacted
phases.description: The lead student delivers the report: 88-year-old male, unwitnessed arrest, no shock advised at every AED analysis, high-quality CPR with OPA and BVM ventilation in progress, family adamant that a physician-signed DNR exists but unable to produce any document, bracelet, or POA paperwork. Medical control answers: "Medic 8, received. Continue with full resuscitation efforts. If the family happens to locate the valid, signed DNR order, you may cease efforts at that time. Otherwise, continue the code." That order maps exactly onto the protocols: resuscitation proceeds until additional information clarifies the picture, and both the DNR and Termination protocols pre-authorize the off-ramp — if CPR has been initiated and a valid exclusion is SUBSEQUENTLY verified, CPR may be discontinued with medical direction. The crew should also recognize where this code is heading if nothing changes: the Termination protocol permits ceasing efforts in asystole after 20 minutes without ROSC when EtCO2 is under 20 mmHg, with all clinicians in agreement and medical direction consulted — for this crew, that decision runs through medical control, not the field. And through all of it, the family remains part of the crew's patient load — kept informed of what is being done, offered support. The scenario ends here, after the medical control call, per the summative design. The documentation burden is real: the verbal DNR claim, who made it, the request for the document, and the medical control order all belong in the report.
phases.triggerCondition: The lead student contacts medical control with a clear, concise report. Medical control responds: "Medic 8, received. Continue with full resuscitation efforts. If the family happens to locate the valid, signed DNR order, you may cease efforts at that time. Otherwise, continue the code."

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA in place; BVM ventilation continues without interrupting compressions
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No spontaneous pulse; high-quality compressions ongoing with rotating compressors; EtCO2 25 mmHg
otherFindings: Medical control order received and repeated back: continue full resuscitation; cease only if valid signed DNR produced
AED continues to advise no shock at each analysis; no ROSC
Son still attempting to reach the lawyer's office; no document has surfaced
Crew member remains with the wife, explaining what is being done
Crew aware of termination criteria should efforts remain ineffective: asystole, 20 minutes, EtCO2 less than 20 mmHg, crew consensus, medical direction
SCENARIO ENDS after the medical control call — proceed to debrief

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue full resuscitation per medical direction — no valid exclusion has been produced
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Inclusion Criteria 3 — medical control's order and the protocol say the same thing: with the validity of the alleged order unresolved, resuscitation proceeds until additional information clarifies the best course of action.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If there is question about the validity of the form/instrument, the best course of action is to proceed with the resuscitation until additional information can be obtained to clarify the best course of action.

expectedActions.shortAction: If a valid signed DNR is later produced and verified, CPR may be discontinued
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Assessment 2 — starting CPR was not an irreversible commitment. The protocol explicitly allows discontinuation if a valid exclusion to resuscitation is subsequently verified, with medical direction contacted as needed — which is exactly the contingency medical control just authorized.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If CPR has been initiated and a valid exclusion to resuscitation has been subsequently verified, CPR may be discontinued, and medical direction contacted as needed.

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize this as a Termination-protocol situation: resuscitation begun, DNR order alleged
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Termination of Resuscitative Efforts Inclusion Criteria 2 — the termination guideline is written for precisely this case: resuscitation underway when a DNR or other actionable medical order comes to light. Knowing which protocol governs the off-ramp is part of running this code correctly.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Inclusion Criteria: When resuscitation has begun and it is found that the patient has a DNR order or other actionable medical order (e.g., POLST/MOLST form).

expectedActions.shortAction: Know termination criteria: asystole, no ROSC after 20 min AND EtCO2 <20 mmHg — via medical direction
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Termination of Resuscitative Efforts Patient Management 1c — if no document surfaces and no shock is ever advised, this resuscitation has a protocol-defined endpoint: 20 minutes without ROSC with EtCO2 below 20 mmHg, all clinicians in agreement, medical direction consulted. The crew should be tracking elapsed time and EtCO2 with that horizon in mind — and for this crew the termination decision itself runs through medical control.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Resuscitation may be terminated in asystole and slow wide complex PEA if there is No return of spontaneous circulation after 20 minutes in the absence of hypothermia AND The EtCO2 is less than 20 mmHg. All EMS clinicians involved in the patient's care agree that discontinuation of the resuscitation is appropriate. Consider contacting medical direction before termination of resuscitative efforts.

expectedActions.shortAction: Keep the family informed of what is being done; offer support resources
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Termination of Resuscitative Efforts Treatment 2–3 — the family is part of the crew's responsibility. The son and wife believe the crew is violating their father's wishes; keeping them informed, and offering support such as clergy or other family, is the protocol-grounded version of the compassionate communication this summative tests.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Focus attention on the family and/or bystanders. Explain the rationale for termination. Consider support for family members such as other family, friends, clergy, faith leaders, or chaplains.

expectedActions.shortAction: Document the DNR claim in detail plus names and contact info of family on scene
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Key Documentation Elements — the report must capture the resuscitation-limiting information relied on (here, a verbal claim with no producible document) and the identities of the significant bystanders who made it. This documentation is the legal record of why full resuscitation proceeded.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: Detailed description of the valid exclusion to resuscitation documentation used to guide resuscitation including a copy of the document if possible. Names/contact information for significant bystanders.

phases.name: CPR withheld on verbal DNR
phases.description: The crew took the son's word for it. No compressions, no pads, no ventilations — two providers standing in a quiet bedroom while a potentially resuscitatable patient accumulates downtime, waiting for a document that is in a safe deposit box across town. This is the critical failure of the summative. The MATC DNR protocol never authorizes this: its entry requirement is a document or bracelet IMMEDIATELY AVAILABLE, its validity test requires an intact, state-conforming order displaying the patient's name, and its instruction for any case where validity is in question is to proceed with resuscitation. The cardiac arrest protocol's exclusion applies only to an IDENTIFIABLE DNR order — and nothing has been identified, only described. Every minute that passes unrepaired makes the physiologic hole deeper: EtCO2 will start lower, and the 20-minute termination clock will eventually be reached without the patient ever having received the resuscitation the protocol owed him — every element of it, compressions, AED analysis, and ventilations, currently owed and undelivered. The recovery move is available at any moment and is written verbatim in the protocol's Patient Safety Considerations: initiate CPR immediately and contact medical direction. The instructor should let the discomfort build — the silence in the room IS the lesson — and reward the student who breaks it by moving to the chest.

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize the error — a verbal claim is not an immediately available document or bracelet
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Inclusion Criteria 1 — the protocol's threshold is physical and present: a document or identification bracelet immediately available. A description of a document elsewhere fails the threshold no matter how sincere the describer. Withholding resuscitation on that basis has no protocol support.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients must have one of the following documents or a valid alternative (such as identification bracelet indicating wishes) immediately available.

expectedActions.shortAction: Cardiac arrest protocol excludes only IDENTIFIABLE DNR orders — none has been identified
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Exclusion Criteria 2 — the arrest protocol steps aside only for an identifiable DNR or equivalent. With nothing identified, this patient is inside the cardiac arrest protocol, and every element of it — compressions, AED analysis, ventilations — is currently owed and undelivered.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Exclusion Criteria: Patients with identifiable Do Not Resuscitate (or equivalent such as POLST) order.

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate CPR immediately and contact medical direction — the protocol's exact instruction
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Patient Safety Considerations — the recovery from this error is written in one sentence of the protocol, and it has two verbs: start CPR now, and put the gray-zone question where it belongs, with medical direction. The student who executes this sentence converts a failed scenario into a delayed-but-recovered one.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Do Not Resuscitate Status/Advance Directives/Healthcare Power of Attorney (POA) Status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: In cases where the patient's status is unclear and the appropriateness of withholding resuscitation efforts is questioned, EMS personnel should initiate CPR immediately and contact medical direction.

transitions.condition: The crew recognizes that no valid exclusion to resuscitation exists, explains to the family that without the physical signed order they are required to act, and initiates CPR — several minutes later than the protocol demanded.

phases.name: Delayed CPR started
phases.description: The crew found their footing — "I understand this is difficult. Without the signed order here, we are required to begin" — and went to work. Everything the cardiac arrest protocol asks of this crew now happens, just late: compressions while the AED is applied, analysis returning "No shock advised," and airway management — OPA, oxygen, BVM — that never interrupts the chest. The physiology keeps score of the delay: initial EtCO2 comes up to only 18 mmHg — a number that now sits below the 20 mmHg line the Termination protocol will use at the 20-minute mark — a concrete, protocol-anchored way for the debrief to show that minutes of hesitation cost real prognosis. Medical direction still needs to be contacted about the unverified DNR, and the delayed start itself now belongs in the documentation: MATC mandates a QI review of every patient who receives CPR, and time-to-first-CPR is one of the protocol's named performance measures. The scenario ends in this branch with the resuscitation running and an honest debrief ahead: the destination was always the same — the only thing the hesitation changed was how much of the patient's chance survived the trip.
phases.triggerCondition: After minutes of standing by, the crew recognizes that no valid exclusion exists, explains their duty to the family with empathy, and initiates full resuscitation — delayed. Initial EtCO2 reflects the accumulated downtime.

expectedActions.shortAction: Begin compressions now while the second rescuer sets up the AED
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 1 — the sequence is unchanged by the delay: compressions immediately, AED applied in parallel, analysis as soon as the device is ready. Late is recoverable; never is not.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Initiate chest compressions in cases with no bystander chest compressions or take over compressions from bystanders while a second rescuer is setting up the AED or defibrillator. For adults and children with unwitnessed cardiac arrest or for whom an AED is not immediately available, it is reasonable that CPR be initiated while the defibrillator equipment is being retrieved and applied and that defibrillation, if indicated, be attempted as soon as the device is ready for use.

expectedActions.shortAction: Analyze with the AED — no shock advised; resume 2-minute compression cycles
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 6 — "no shock advised" earns an immediate return to compressions, cycling analysis every two minutes.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Continue the cycle of chest compressions for 2 minutes, followed by rhythm analysis and defibrillation of shockable rhythms.

expectedActions.shortAction: OPA and ventilations without interrupting compressions — maximal oxygen during CPR
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Treatment 6a and Airway Management Treatment 2b/3c — the delayed resuscitation uses the same airway strategy as the timely one: an OPA for the patient without a gag reflex, maximal oxygen, and nothing that interrupts the chest.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The airway management strategy should not interrupt compressions. During CPR, maximal oxygen supplementation should be provided.

expectedActions.shortAction: Contact medical direction about the unverified DNR while resuscitation continues
expectedActions.rationale: MATC DNR/Advance Directives Patient Safety Considerations — the second verb of the protocol's recovery sentence. The gray-zone question of the alleged DNR still needs medical direction's input; starting CPR did not resolve it, it just made the patient safe while it gets resolved.

expectedActions.shortAction: Document times precisely — QI review of every CPR case will examine time to first CPR
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Cardiac Arrest Key Considerations 15 and Performance Measures — every resuscitation gets a medical-director-overseen QI review, and time to first CPR is a named performance measure. The honest record of the delay is both a legal necessity and the raw material for the debrief this summative exists to produce.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The EMS agency must perform a Quality Improvement (QI) review of care and outcome, overseen by the agency medical director, for every patient that receives CPR. Performance Measures: Time to scene. Time to patient. Time to first CPR.
